E0190.summary: In a passage quoted from Eudoxus, a veiled name for the spirits of the bodies, which feed the two Mercuries and prepare the King's bath.
E0190.body: Quoted from Eudoxus, who explains the expression himself: “the blood of innocents whose throats are cut; that is to say, the spirits of the bodies” [IV.3 ¶10]. In that passage these spirits feed the two Mercuries and prepare the King's bath. Asserted identity: = the spirits of the bodies [IV.3 ¶10].

E0191.summary: A name for the secret product of the work: Khunrath equates it with the gold of the philosophers; the Hunting of the Greene Lyon makes it the King's only food.
E0191.body:
**Khunrath** (quoted) names it beside the universal tincture as what he received: “the blood of the Lion, which is the gold of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶81]. Asserted identity: = gold of the philosophers [I.1 ¶81].

**The Hunting of the Greene Lyon** (quoted verse) describes it as the 'secret' drawn off after Lion, Sol and Luna unite and form a skin: “A right good secret withouten any nay: Wych must serve to doe thee good’ For yt ys the Lyons Blood:” [III.1 ¶65]. It is the King's only food, given after he rises from the dead: “And tis as strange that thys Kings food, Can be nothing but thys Lyons Blood;” [III.1 ¶65]; and it is worked with Luna or Sol to prepare the ferments [III.1 ¶65]. Asserted identity: = a right good secret [III.1 ¶65]. A reader noted that the same passage may also call it the King's Father and Mother; this is uncertain.

E0192.summary: Author in Ashmole's collection whose Blossoms and Camp of Philosophy Atwood cites for the subject's many names and for the threefold magistery.
E0192.body: Atwood counts **Bloomfield's Blossoms** among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64], and names Bloomfield as a witness to rings made of Kelly's gold [I.1 ¶66]. From the **Camp of Philosophy**, book I (in Ashmole), she illustrates the many names of the subject: “It is a privy quintessence; keepe it well in minde” [I.2 ¶41; I.2 n38]. Its Conclusion (in Theatrum Chemicum Brit.) supports her account of the threefold magistery, the Dragon, the blackness and the appearing of Phoebus: “Our magistery is Three, Two, and One” [IV.2 ¶36; IV.2 n25].

E0193.summary: In Vaughan's quoted account, the descent or incorporation of the finished Stone cast on molten gold, which abates the gold's strength to fix a projection ratio.
E0193.body: Quoted from Vaughan: casting the finished Stone on molten gold so that the gold abates its strength, in order to fix a usable ratio for projection. “This descent or incorporation, some wise authors have called a bodily fermentation” [IV.3 ¶22]. Asserted identity: = descent or incorporation [IV.3 ¶22].

E0194.summary: In quoted authorities, the hard, dry or dead part of the matter that imprisons the spirit or fire and must be dissolved, rotted and glorified.
E0194.body:
Three quoted voices use the term:

- **Eirenaeus**: the hard, dry body in which the fire is imprisoned, rotted by 'our water': “which in the hard and dry body is imprisoned” [III.1 ¶14]. A gloss in the passage (whose voice is unclear) makes it the ethereal body: “by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)” [III.1 ¶14].
- **Eudoxus**: what remains after the Water is distilled off: “the Body remains in the bottom of the vessel, like a dead, black, and dredgy earth” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is not to be despised, and must be wholly dissolved and glorified. He names it Adam: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
- **The Scholiast** (reported by Atwood): “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” [I.3 n38], glossed as “the bodies (i.e., the sensible and vegetable media of life)” [I.3 n38], which must be dissolved into their radical source.

Asserted identities: = ethereal body [III.1 ¶14]; = Adam [IV.3 ¶7]; = the sensible and vegetable media of life [I.3 n38].

E0195.summary: Atwood's gloss in the Appendix: the impure natural-born vital spirit.
E0195.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The body of brass is the impure natural-born vital spirit.” [APP ¶52]. Asserted identity: = impure natural-born vital spirit.

E0196.summary: In the quoted Adept, the body which the Preparing Spirit dissolves and cleanses, and from which a tinging spirit is extracted.
E0196.body: Quoted from the Adept: the Preparing Spirit “dissolves the body of Light” [IV.1 ¶10], cleansing it, and a tinging spirit is then extracted from it.

E0197.summary: Writer Atwood treats as the plainest experiential exponent of the mystery, cited throughout for the Tincture, the Three Principles and divine manifestation, though she judges him theosophical rather than intellectual.
E0197.body:
Atwood calls Jacob Boehme the plainest exponent of the mystery from experience, with explicit pointers to the physical basis of magic and the material of the stone, citing the Aurora, Three Principles, Mysterium Magnum, Tree of Life, Turned Eye and Epistles [I.1 ¶68; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n77]. She qualifies this: his revelation is theosophical, not intellectual [I.1 ¶70]. His writings alarmed alchemists by applying alchemy openly to human life [II.1 ¶9].

**The Work.** From the Tract. Aur., Epistles and Forty Questions she takes the white and red stages and the concealment under the Seal of God: “the Work is easy and simple, but the wisdom therein is great and the greatest mystery” [II.1 ¶24; II.1 n20]. Forty Questions 17 gives the core operation, Sol and Luna brought through death at the cross and reconceived: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48; III.1 n53]; Atwood says it comprehends 'the end and beginning of the Sacred Art'. The Three Principles supplies the Antimonial Spirit and the Invisible Mercury: “the agent in the preparation of this spirit, continues Bohme, is the Invisible Mercury” [II.1 ¶20], and the disorder of arterial blood [II.1 ¶21; II.1 n17]; the Generation of the Three Principles gives the creation of a cloud condensed into water: “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. His account of the Tincture, which “is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16], is endorsed as agreeing with the ancient Kabalah [III.2 ¶17]; the Turned Eye gives 'modern testimony' of his illumination: “the gate was opened to me” [III.2 ¶16]. The operator must first “seek God’s love and grace, and resign up themselves to become wholly one with that” [III.1 ¶39]; Atwood qualifies that the divine cannot exactly be given into possession [III.1 ¶40]. On contrition and the Tincture: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24]. He is among Adepts comparing the work to the Creed [IV.3 ¶27].

**Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer): he knew the mystery by experienced in-seeing whereby he became it [APP ¶117]; the deepest writer on ontological subjects, less scientific than the Platonists but more descriptive, awakening, suggestive [APP ¶62]; his three primary forms and doctrine of the Absolute Will read as expressions of conscious experience of the creative mystery [APP ¶65]; surpassing the Neo-Platonists on the Life Center [APP ¶122]. His Law of Divine Manifestation, the order the Hermetic Work imitates: “An Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to introduce the No Thing into Something, that the Will might feel and find and behold itself” [APP ¶73]; cited for the Sulphur, Salt and Mercury nomenclature [APP ¶81]; 'in the Experience' of the uncreated beyond the metaphysicians, though they surpassed him in scientific intuition [APP ¶96]. Also: the Third Principle as medium of perceiving the First, “the sidereal and elementary birth” [APP ¶27]; the Three-fold Life on will begetting a being out of its own image [APP ¶36]; his Mercurius, or spirit of the Sound, for the harmony freed from the lower life [APP ¶49]; Signatura Rerum on knowing things in their roots on entering the Signature, “through the principle in the sound with the voice” [APP ¶63]; with de St Martin, source of 'the Crown', and contrasted with Engelbrecht as penetrating surfaces, his body swallowed up with Light [APP ¶104; APP ¶105]; the bitterness of self-life from which nature shields us, “the bitter anguish of the driving wheel of existence” [APP ¶154].

E0198.summary: Atwood's term for the magical bond that everywhere shuts up Nature's Inner Light and principle of perfection, which Nature cannot loosen herself.
E0198.body: Atwood speaks of “the bond of coagulation by which her Inner Light and principle of perfection is everywhere shut up” [III.2 ¶61]. Nature cannot loosen this bond by herself [III.2 ¶61]; the context suggests that loosening it is the task of the art.

E0199.summary: An enigma which, Atwood reports, the adepts claimed as referring to the occult material of the art.
E0199.body: Atwood reports that the adepts claimed the Bononian Enigma as referring to the occult material of the art [I.1 ¶20; I.1 ¶21]. It opens “Nec vir, nec mulier, nec androgyna,” [I.1 n29] (ours: 'Neither man, nor woman, nor androgyne').

E0200.summary: Book Atwood quotes as epigraph and illustration: wisdom as water, whiteness, the Radical Essence, and metal mountains melting before the Elect One.
E0200.body: Atwood uses the Book of Enoch for epigraph and illustration. Chapter xl.1 heads III.3: “Wisdom is poured forth like water, and glory faileth not before Him for ever.” [III.3 ¶2]. Chapters 46 and 41 illustrate whiteness, “the Ancient of Days, whose head was like wool” [III.2 ¶4; III.2 n6], and the seer's vision of the Radical Essence, winds, clouds and the cloud before creation [III.2 ¶12; III.2 n12]. Section 109, on rain, dew and metal mountains melting before the Elect One, is given without comment: “ye that are capable to comprehend the Elect One” [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n8].

E0202.summary: Book whose first chapter Atwood compares with the building of Solomon's Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.
E0202.body: Atwood quotes chapter 1, “with the Fiery Letters of the Law, He engraved the empty, and the void, and the obscure mind” [IV.2 ¶33; IV.2 n21], and compares it with the building of Solomon's Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.

E0203.summary: Book Atwood praises in the Appendix as the best description of Wisdom as man's exemplar.
E0203.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood calls it the best description of Wisdom as man's exemplar [APP ¶90]. Cited together with the Poemander, chapter 11, verse 22 illustrates the whole world held before the divine vision, as before one who has the Principle: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

E0204.summary: Old sources whose unguents made from fats, hair and similar things are rejected in the passage citing them.
E0204.body: Cited critically: the unguents made from fats, hair and the like, “which are written in the books of our fathers” [I.3 ¶53], are rejected.

E0205.summary: Modern authority who lauds the Isaacs and, with Homberg and Boyle, held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.
E0205.body: Atwood cites Boorhaave for the Isaacs' reputation: he lauds them and seems acquainted with occult science [I.1 ¶58]. With Homberg and Boyle he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

E0206.summary: Atwood's gloss: the Philosopher's Stone, made from the Citrine extracted from the Red.
E0206.body: Atwood glosses the term in a footnote: “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52], made from the Citrine extracted from the Red. Asserted identity: = Philosopher's Stone.

E0207.summary: Modern figure rumoured to have known Philalethes, and named among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.
E0207.body: Boyle is rumoured, uncertainly, to have been intimate with Philalethes [I.1 ¶73]. With Homberg and Boerhaave he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

E0208.summary: A veiled name in quoted authorities: for Hermes the Art of the permanent water; for Albertus the occult Nature to be washed, dissolved and fixed.
E0208.body:
**Hermes** (quoted): “the Art of this permanent water is our brass” [I.3 ¶43]; Democritus draws out the 'Fixed Brass' bodily: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily, writes our Abderite” [I.3 n53].

**Albertus** (quoted) uses it for the occult Nature: “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass” [IV.1 ¶4], which is to be washed pure and clean, then dissolved, distilled, sublimed, calcined and fixed.

Asserted identities: = Art of this permanent water [I.3 ¶43]; = occult Nature [IV.1 ¶4]. See also body of brass, Brazen Body.

E0209.summary: In Hermes as quoted, the body to be burned with exceeding great fire, exemplified by Democritus drawing out the 'Fixed Brass'.
E0209.body: Quoted from Hermes: “Burn then the Brazen Body with an exceeding great fire” [I.3 ¶42]. Democritus, exemplifying this juncture, draws out the 'Fixed Brass' and works it on the coals [I.3 ¶42].

E0210.summary: Atwood's image of the barrier surrounding 'our Heaven' that must be scaled and passed before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.
E0210.body: Atwood: “this is that Brazen Wall celebrated by Antiquity, which surrounds our Heaven and must be scaled” [IV.1 ¶4]. It must be passed through before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.

E0211.summary: Atwood's gloss: the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit, finally gathered into accord with its first source.
E0211.body: Atwood glosses the term: “by the brethren, the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit” [I.3 n50], which are finally gathered into accord with the spirit's first source.

E0212.summary: A group voice whose phrase names the only builders who 'erect structures in the air'.
E0212.body: The phrase of the Brethren for the only builders who 'erect structures in the air': “Master mason, of Grand Architects” [IV.2 ¶14].

E0213.summary: A fraternity which Atwood says agreed about the Matter and found it experimentally; she quotes their letter and the Matter's speeches.
E0213.body: Atwood says the Christian brotherhood of the Rosy Cross agreed concerning the Matter, searched Nature experimentally, found it and used it [III.2 ¶60]. A letter circulated under their name gives an allegory of the initiatory passage (mountain, beasts, night, guide, courage): “There is a mountain situated in the midst of the earth or center of the world” [II.3 ¶31; II.3 ¶32]. From the Latin original of the Fraternity, as given in Vaughan's Coelum Terrae, she quotes speeches of the Matter as Goddess (First Matter, Eagle and Lion, five gates) and as Dragon or Mercury: “I am a Goddess for beauty and extraction” [III.3 ¶62; III.3 n45].

E0214.summary: In Hermes as quoted, that to which the son is to be joined, called Jupiter and a hidden secret.
E0214.body: Quoted from Hermes: “join the son to Buba, which is Jupiter and a hidden secret” [I.3 ¶37]. Asserted identity: = Jupiter.

E0215.summary: Boehme's word, glossed in the quoted passage itself as the ground or original foundation.
E0215.body: Quoted from Boehme, who glosses it: “the Bysse, or ground or original foundation” [III.2 ¶16]. Asserted identity: = ground or original foundation.

E0216.summary: Said of Lully's mind and of the art itself: veiled, full of mysteries, not to be understood according to the letter.
E0216.body: Atwood says one must “possess the key of his cabalistic mind” [I.1 ¶48] to understand Lully's obscure alchemical works. Artephius (quoted) applies it to the art: “For is not our art cabalistic” [I.1 ¶84], full of mysteries, not taught openly, not to be understood according to the letter.

E0217.summary: Atwood's name for a practice of the time of concealing truth by displacing order, inverting and dispersing repetitions.
E0217.body: Atwood blames the displacement of verses from their original order on “the mischievous cabalistic method in vogue at that time” [I.1 ¶64], and traces to it the artifices used to hide the truth, such as inversion of order and dispersed repetition: “A variety of artifices according to the cabalistic method” [I.1 ¶82].

forms: cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience
E0218.summary: Ancient sources whose reported view grounds man's rank in a Divine Reason and latent Faculty of Wisdom; Atwood says it was once proved but is now beyond evidence.
E0218.body: Atwood reports their view that man's rank rests on a Divine Reason and a latent Faculty of Wisdom: “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32]. She says this was once proved but is now beyond present evidence [II.1 ¶32].

E0219.summary: Figures Atwood names as the god dead and revived among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians.
E0219.body: Atwood names Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis and Osiris as instances of the god dead and revived, among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians [III.3 ¶69].

forms: Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus
E0220.summary: Heroes Atwood says passed the same ordeal, their adventures read as records of the soul's struggle with her inner enemies.
E0220.body: Atwood names Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules and Orpheus as heroes who passed the same ordeal, and reads their adventures as records of the soul's struggle with her inner enemies [III.3 ¶71].
